new_statements.quote: All the languages dealt with here (W B R S) have, in addition to the types of syllables already described, other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable. Such weak syllables usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur. The tone on such syllables tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch in all four languages. [...] It is noteworthy that of the four languages here studied, Siamese has by far the greatest number of such weak syllables, Red Tai somewhat fewer, Black Tai still fewer, and in White Tai they are infrequent.
new_statements.citation: Gedney, William J. 1964. "A comparative sketch of White, Black and Red Tai." The Social Science Review (Bangkok), special number: 1-47; reprinted in R. J. Bickner, J. Hartmann, T. J. Hudak & P. Peyasantiwong (eds), Selected Papers on Comparative Tai Studies (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 29), Ann Arbor: University of Michigan, 1989, 415-462.
new_statements.locator: p. 421 of the 1989 reprint (PDF page 7), paragraph following the Red Tai checked-syllable tones; scanned text in lines 362-375
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Red Tai (Tay Daeng, which Ferlus 2008 identifies with Tay Thanh/Man Thanh) is a tone language whose normal syllables each carry a distinctive tone; the only stress statement is that a minor prefixed syllable (usually short a) has weak stress and a neutralized mid-level tone, so in such words prominence lies on the final, full (toned) syllable. Ferlus 2008, the only description of Nghệ An Tay Thanh itself, states the word is strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak syllables 'usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur'; the phenomenon is described as infrequent in the basic vocabulary, and Gedney says it 'would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language'. Later (pp. 454, 458-459) tone/vowel irregularities in some words (e.g. 'one', 'how many', classifier to1, 'not', 'equal') are attributed to reduction 'in unstressed position'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: monosyllabic words carry a full tone; sesquisyllabic words consist of a weak-stressed prefixed minor syllable plus a normal (toned) syllable. The remark is made for all four languages compared (White, Black, Red Tai, Siamese); the Red Tai data are from Ban Na Yon, Sam Neua province, Laos, elicited in Vientiane in 1964 ('only a few hours' of work, p. 418). No word-level stress rule beyond this is given; nothing on phrase stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Identity caveat, substantial. The quoted stress statement is Gedney's, about Red Tai (tay4 leeng1) of Ban Na Yon, Sam Neua province, Laos, which under ISO/Glottolog is Tai Daeng [tyr] = taid1249 (Tai Daeng-Meuay), not [tmm]. The link to tait1248 rests on Ferlus 2008 (the only description of the Nghệ An variety), who states that the Tay Daeng 'sont appelés Tay Thanh ou Man Thanh par les Vietnamiens', titles his section '4. Tay Daeng (ou Tay Thanh)', uses Gedney 1964 as one of its sources, and reports that the 5-tone system of Tay Thanh of Con Cuông (B2 = C1 merged) also characterises the Tay Daeng dialects of Thanh Hóa and Laos per Gedney 1964. Ferlus's own Tay Thanh description (Con Cuông, Nghệ An) is silent on stress (word 'strictement monosyllabique CV(C)/T'). Vietnamese usage: Tày Thanh = Man Thanh = Tay Nhài, Nghệ An and Thanh Hóa. If the catalog keys strictly by ISO code, file the Gedney statement under taid1249 and mark tait1248 as accessible-description-silent-on-stress (Ferlus 2008).

sources.note: p. 421: all four languages (White, Black, Red Tai, Siamese) have, besides normal toned syllables, 'other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable', usually with short a, whose tone 'tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch'; Red Tai has 'somewhat fewer' of these than Siamese. sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2008. "The Tai dialects of Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong)", in Diller, Edmondson & Luo (eds), The Tai-Kadai Languages, Routledge, 298-315. Read in the author's updated French version "Les dialectes tai du Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong)", HAL halshs-01617791 (Oct 2017), 24 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey); publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: Silent on stress. Section 3 states the basic word in Tay Daeng (= Tay Thanh), Tay Yo and Tay Muong is 'strictement monosyllabique: CV(C)/T'; section 4.3 gives the 5-tone system of Tay Thanh of Con Cuong (B2 = C1 merged). Explicitly: 'Les Tay Daeng... sont appelés Tay Thanh ou Man Thanh par les Vietnamiens' (p. 3) and cites Gedney 1964 as a source for its Tay Daeng data.
